chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from a number of our companions from Ahmad ibn Muhammad from 'Amr ibn 'Uthman from Muhammad ibn 'Udhafir said:

I entered with my father upon Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), and my father asked him about the Tasbih of Fatimah (peace be upon her). He said: 'Allahu Akbar' until he counted thirty-four times. Then he said: 'Al-hamdu lillah' until he reached sixty-six. Then he said: 'Subhan Allah' until he reached one hundred, counting them with his hand as a single total.

key_terms.اللَّهُ أَكْبَرُ: Allahu Akbar (God is the Greatest), the first phrase in the tasbih
key_terms.الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ: Al-hamdu lillah (Praise be to God), the second phrase in the tasbih
key_terms.تَسْبِيحِ فَاطِمَ: Tasbih of Fatimah, a specific devotional dhikr attributed to Fatimah al-Zahra
key_terms.سُبْحَانَ اللَّهِ: Subhan Allah (Glory be to God), the third phrase in the tasbih
key_terms.يُحْصِيهَا بِيَدِهِ: Counting them with his hand, indicating the method of keeping track of the recitations

ai.seo_question: What is the exact recitation count and formula for the Tasbih of Fatimah according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: Recorded in Shaykh al-Tusi’s *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, this hadith establishes the precise numerical structure of the Tasbih of Fatimah, a practice deeply rooted in Shia tradition as a means of spiritual purification and gratitude. The specific counts—34, 66, and 100—reflect a balanced rhythm of glorification, praise, and transcendence, often recited after the obligatory Fajr prayer to anchor the believer’s day in remembrance of Allah.
